concepts-american-vs-european-options.summary: American options can be exercised any time up to expiration; European only at expiration. Differences cover price, dividends, typical markets, liquidity, and physical versus cash settlement; European style spares sellers from early assignment.

rules.text: Option sellers who want to avoid early assignment may prefer European-style (typically index) options.

mechanics.point: American options can be exercised early, including to capture a dividend before the ex-dividend date; European cannot, so no early assignment for sellers.
American style is common for U.S. stocks and ETFs; European style is common for index options and futures-related products.
Physical settlement delivers the underlying (typical of American stock options); cash settlement pays the difference in cash (typical of index options and European style).
Settlement price is the underlying's price at exercise or expiration, used to compute value; for European options it is fixed at expiration.
American options tend to be more liquid in popular U.S. stocks and ETFs; European options are less liquid for single stocks but liquid in index and futures options.
American options are typically priced slightly higher than European on average because of the early-exercise right.

concepts-an-intro-to-the-greeks.summary: Defines the five main option Greeks (delta, gamma, theta, vega, rho) and the minor second-order Greeks, with how each behaves by moneyness and time, and why they matter for sellers and buyers alike.
unmapped: minor Greeks (vomma, speed, zomma, color, ultima, charm, lambda)

mechanics.point: Delta is the option price change per $1 move in the underlying: calls run 0 to 1, puts -1 to 0, ATM options sit near 0.50 in absolute value, ITM deltas drift toward 1 and OTM deltas toward 0 as expiration nears.
Gamma is how much delta changes per $1 underlying move; it is larger for ATM and ITM options than OTM, so their deltas shift faster. Traders watch it at position and portfolio level.

Theta is daily time decay; options generally lose value as expiry approaches, and decay accelerates near expiration so shorter-dated options carry higher theta. Long options held a long time can lose heavily to decay.
Vega is the price change per 1 point change in implied volatility; owned calls and puts gain when IV rises. It is larger for longer-dated and ATM options than for near-dated or OTM ones.

Rho is the price change per 1% move in interest rates; positive for long calls and short puts, negative for short calls and long puts. It matters more for longer-dated and ATM options but is often ignored because rates stay flat for long stretches.

Positive delta means bullish bias (long calls, short puts); negative delta means bearish bias (short calls, long puts). Delta can also be read as share equivalency, hedge ratio, or chance of finishing ITM.
All Greeks are dynamic and change with the underlying price, time and each other. The Greeks matter to option sellers as much as buyers since they measure risk for any position or portfolio.

concepts-assignment.summary: How option assignment works: exercise, OCC random allocation, conversion to 100 shares, what makes assignment more likely, and that the premium is kept.

rules.text: Short option writers should be ready for assignment at any time until expiration; it is never certain, the holder decides.
Writing options is meant for experienced traders since shorts carry 100 shares of long or short stock risk.

mechanics.point: When a holder exercises, the OCC randomly passes the notice to a member firm, which picks a client short the same series (underlying, strike, expiration).
Assignment converts the option into 100 shares per contract: short call becomes short stock, short put becomes long stock, at the strike; long call becomes long stock, long put short stock.
Assignment happens when the market is closed, not intraday.
Assignment is more likely for ITM options, near expiration, and for ITM short calls when the upcoming dividend exceeds remaining extrinsic value; more extrinsic value means lower likelihood.
OTM options are unlikely to be assigned because shares can be traded at a better price in the market.
The writer keeps the premium whether or not assigned, but it may not offset the loss from assignment.
American-style options can be exercised up to expiration date close; timing details depend on the exchange.

Selling an option contract; same as shorting a put or call.

concepts-backwardation.summary: Defines backwardation as a futures curve where later contracts price below nearer ones or spot, contrasts it with contango, lists causes, roll-yield and spread approaches, and risks such as thin liquidity and sudden reversals.

rules.text: In a backwardized market, a long holder may sell the near contract and buy a longer-dated one at a lower price (roll yield), or exit and wait for contango to return.
Assess liquidity before entering backwardized markets, since wider bid-ask spreads and reduced volume make fills harder.
Expect higher-than-average volatility and possible swift reversal back to contango; keep disciplined risk management in all curve conditions.

mechanics.point: In backwardation, nearer prices exceed later-dated futures prices; in contango (the normal state in most markets) later contracts are priced higher, reflecting inflation and uncertainty.
Backwardation arises from short supply and demand for immediate delivery, widespread expectation of falling prices (e.g., recession), supply disruptions, weather or geopolitical events.
Futures spreads (long one expiry, short another) profit if the contracts converge and lose if they diverge.

terms.definition: A futures curve where later-dated contracts trade below nearer-dated ones or spot.
The usual curve shape where later-dated futures trade above spot or nearer contracts.
Gain from rolling an expiring futures position into a cheaper later contract in backwardation.
The current price for immediate delivery.

concepts-bear-call-spread.summary: Bear call spread sells a lower-strike call and buys a higher-strike call for a net credit; defined risk and profit, wins if price stays below the short strike, helped by falling IV and time decay. Page gives no tastylive-specific rules.

concepts-bear-put-spread.summary: Bear put spread (long put vertical): buy a higher-strike put, sell a lower-strike put, same expiration, for a net debit. Defined risk and reward for a moderately bearish view; formulas, pros and cons, vega and theta effects.

concepts-beta-weight.summary: Beta weighting converts all positions to one benchmark unit to see portfolio directional exposure; tastylive typically uses SPY, sometimes a sector ETF like QQQ, as a context tool rather than an exact number.

rules.text: Beta weight to SPY when holding mostly liquid mid to large caps correlated with the S&P 500; use a closer benchmark such as QQQ if positions cluster in one sector.
Use beta weighting to keep strategies from relying too much on the market's direction; drop positions that distort the figure.

mechanics.point: Betas are computed from the past five years of data to span varied market environments.
The result is a contextual guide to size, diversity and general risk, not a precise calculation input.

terms.definition: Expressing all positions in one standard benchmark unit to see how the portfolio responds to market moves.

concepts-beta.summary: Beta measures a security's volatility relative to the market (market = 1.0), computed as covariance over variance; page covers high/low/negative beta sectors and using beta for strategy selection and portfolio risk, with caveats.

rules.text: For a high-beta stock expected to swing widely, consider long volatility structures like long straddles or strangles.
For a low-beta stock expected to be stable, consider covered calls or short straddles/strangles.
Mix assets with different betas; adding negative-beta exposure can offset positive-beta option positions in downturns.

mechanics.point: Beta = covariance of the stock's returns with the market divided by the market's variance. A beta of 1.5 implies the stock moves about 50% more than the market, e.g. 1.5% when the S&P moves 1%.

Cyclical sectors (technology, consumer discretionary, energy, financials, industrials) tend to have beta above 1; defensive ones (utilities, staples, healthcare, consumer services, telecom) tend below 1; safe havens like gold or government bonds can show negative beta.
Beta is backward-looking, shifts over time and by sample period, assumes a linear relationship, and may miss sudden shifts, so it should be used with other analysis.

terms.definition: Sensitivity of a security's returns to market returns; a market-risk gauge with the market at 1.0.
An asset that tends to move opposite to the market, offering hedge or diversification value.

concepts-black-swan-event.summary: A black swan is a rare, unpredictable event with outsized, cascading market impact, often arising from hidden systemic weakness amid complacency. Page lists four historic drawdowns and notes VIX spiking to records in two of them.

concepts-broken-wing-butterfly.summary: Broken-wing butterfly is a butterfly with an uneven wide wing, routed for a credit so there is no loss if it expires entirely OTM; page covers P&L formulas, the tastylive credit-only rule, profit targets, and defensive moves.

concepts-cash-settled-options.summary: Cash-settled options pay the in-the-money difference in cash at exercise instead of delivering the underlying; page covers mechanics, benefits like simplicity and lower costs, and contrasts physical delivery.

mechanics.point: Cash-settled options pay (or debit) the difference between strike and the underlying's settlement level instead of moving shares or goods; OTM options expire worthless. Typical for index options, some futures and commodities.
Example: index call with strike 1,000 bought for $30, index at 1,050 at expiry settles for $50, net $20; below 1,000 loses the full $30.
For a short cash-settled option the account is debited the option's settlement value; profit or loss depends on the credit originally collected.

No delivery means lower transaction costs and simpler logistics, and can need less capital than owning the underlying; useful for hedging or speculating without ownership. Not available in every market.

Physical delivery transfers the actual shares or goods on exercise (e.g. equity options deliver stock), bringing storage and handling issues in commodities; some traders prefer it and choose such contracts.

terms.definition: Option that settles by cash payment based on the strike vs underlying level, with no asset delivery.
Settlement by actually transferring the underlying asset on exercise.

concepts-cash-settlement.summary: Cash settlement pays the price difference in cash at expiration instead of delivering the asset; contrasted with physical delivery, with index option and futures examples and benefits like simplicity and lower cost.

mechanics.point: Cash-settled options pay the in-the-money amount times the multiplier at expiration (S&P index option: points ITM times $100); OTM options simply expire worthless.
Physically settled stock options deliver 100 shares per contract on exercise; cash-settled index options never deliver the index.
Futures can be either: WTI crude is physically settled, while index and interest-rate futures are cash-settled.
Cash settlement avoids storage, transport and delivery costs and is described as cheaper and typically more liquid.

terms.definition: Contract resolved by paying the price difference rather than delivering the asset.
Settlement where the underlying asset actually changes hands.

concepts-collar-option.summary: Collar combines long stock, a long OTM put and a short OTM call (same expiry) to bracket outcomes, ideally at zero cost; covers max profit and loss, pros and cons. No tastylive-specific numbers.

strategy_notes.legs: own 100 shares, buy OTM put below price, sell OTM call above price, same expiration
strategy_notes.outlook: protective on a core stock holding; expecting near-term volatility or a correction
strategy_notes.max_profit: (call strike - stock price at entry) plus net credit or minus net debit, per share, times 100
strategy_notes.max_loss: (stock price at entry - put strike) adjusted for net premium, times 100

tasty_setup.dte: same expiration for both options; choose per outlook
tasty_setup.strikes: put below and call above current price; ideal when call premium roughly equals put cost (costless collar)

management.close: can close or let options expire; partial collars (hedge only some shares) are allowed

strategy_notes.accounts: needs 100 shares per collar for full protection
when_to_use: concentrated or legacy stock position you want to keep (taxes, dividends, long-term view) but protect
when_to_avoid: strong rally expected, since upside is capped
mistakes: put costs more than the call, creating a net debit
poorly chosen strikes from misjudging volatility
partial coverage leaves uncovered shares unprotected

rules.text: Pair one collar contract with 100 shares for full protection.
Try to balance put cost with call credit for a cost-neutral collar.
A collar can cover only part of a stock position; unhedged shares keep upside but are unprotected.

mechanics.point: Above the call strike the shares may be called away; below the put strike the put sets a sale floor.

terms.definition: Collar where short call credit offsets long put cost.

concepts-company-earnings.summary: Explains quarterly earnings reports, key metrics (revenue, net income, EPS, margins, guidance, surprises), why stock reactions are uncertain, and how IV rises before and crushes after the report.

rules.text: A good or bad report does not guarantee the stock moves the same way; account for surprise moves in risk sizing.
Sellers aim to benefit from the post-report vol crush; buyers bet on a dramatic move. Both carry amplified risk and need preparation.

mechanics.point: IV rises sharply into the report, inflating near-term expirations that include it, then often collapses afterward.

terms.definition: Net profit allocated to each outstanding share.
Gap between actual results and analyst expectations.
Company projections of future performance.

concepts-contango.summary: Contango is a futures curve where longer-dated contracts trade above spot; seen as the normal state, usually calm with low volatility, while backwardation signals scarcity or expected declines. Volatility futures are not always in contango.

rules.text: Contango can flip to backwardation at any time, so keep disciplined risk management in every environment.

mechanics.point: Contango: futures price above expected spot at expiration (curve slopes up); backwardation is the reverse.

Contango is associated with adequate supply, carrying/storage costs and low price volatility; backwardation arises from expected declines, shortages, supply disruptions, weather or geopolitical events.
Deep contango in volatility futures is characterized as calm or complacent; backwardation goes with elevated implied and realized volatility and less predictability.
A futures spread buying a near contract and selling a later one profits if prices converge and loses if they diverge.

terms.definition: Futures curve where later contracts trade at a premium to spot.
Futures curve where futures trade at a discount to spot.

concepts-correlation.summary: Correlation ranges from -1 to +1 measured historically (at least one month); use it to diversify across non-correlated underlyings, remembering it can break down in crashes. Bullish trades in correlated names add no diversity.

rules.text: Check correlation when adding trades; five bullish positions in positively correlated underlyings provide no real diversification.
Do not rely on correlation in a crash; it can fall apart when markets move sharply up or down.

mechanics.point: Correlation is measured on historical data with a minimum of one month.
Page bands: weak 0.1-0.3, moderate 0.3-0.5, strong 0.5-1.0 (mirrored for negative); between -0.1 and 0.1 means little or no relationship.

terms.definition: Two underlyings tend to move in the same direction.
Two underlyings tend to move in opposite directions.

concepts-covered-call.summary: Covered call pairs 100 shares with one short ATM/OTM call per 100 shares for income in a sideways to mildly bullish view; page gives payoff formulas and the tastylive approach of ~45 DTE, ~30 delta, with roll rules.

strategy_notes.legs: long 100 shares of stock plus short 1 ATM or OTM call per 100 shares
strategy_notes.max_profit: Distance from stock purchase price to the short call strike plus credit received; reached with stock at or above the strike at expiration
strategy_notes.max_loss: Stock going to zero; the loss is on the shares and is cushioned by the call credit
strategy_notes.breakevens: Stock purchase price minus credit received

tasty_setup.dte: about 45 DTE is ideal per their studies
tasty_setup.strikes: sell the most liquid call near the 30 delta
tasty_setup.iv: high IV is the ideal environment
tasty_setup.credit_target: credit must be meaningful; if only about $0.10 is available, consider another strategy or wait for more premium

management.roll: Roll when the bullish assumption is unchanged and little or no extrinsic value remains: buy back the short call and sell the same strike further out. If stock drops, roll the call down to collect more premium and lower max loss and breakeven, but never below the current breakeven.
management.loss_rule: Consider closing if the stock falls a lot and the assumption changes
management.close: Close when the stock has moved well past the short call, since that is near max profit
management.assignment: If it expires ITM the call buyer takes the shares at the strike; upside above strike is forfeited

when_to_use: Own shares and expect sideways or slightly higher price
Want income from premium on an existing holding willing to be sold at the strike
Prefer it over naked stock because it profits when the stock is flat and lowers max loss
when_to_avoid: Very bullish on the stock because the short call caps upside
Call premium is tiny (about $0.10)
mistakes: Rolling the call down past the current breakeven can lock in a loss if the stock rebounds and leaves the call ITM

rules.text: Enter covered calls at roughly 45 DTE.
Sell the most liquid call near 30 delta for a high-probability trade that still gains if the stock rises.
Favor low-priced, high-volatility stocks for this strategy.
If the call would only collect about $0.10, consider another strategy or wait for richer premium.
Roll the short call out in time at the same strike when the thesis is intact and extrinsic value is nearly gone.
If stock falls, roll the call down for more credit, but never below the current breakeven.
Close when the stock has moved well beyond the short call (near max profit) or when a big drop changes the outlook.

mechanics.point: One contract covers 100 shares; selling 10 calls puts a 1,000 share position at risk of being called away. If ITM at expiration the seller must deliver shares at the strike.

terms.definition: Long stock with a short call against it so the shares cover any assignment.

concepts-debit-spreads.summary: Debit spreads (bull call, bear put) cost a net debit, cap profit and loss, suit moderate directional views, and are contrasted with credit spreads on cash flow, volatility and time decay.

strategy_notes.legs: call version: buy lower-strike call, sell higher-strike call; put version: buy higher-strike put, sell lower-strike put; same expiration
strategy_notes.max_profit: strike width minus net debit
strategy_notes.max_loss: net debit paid

management.defend: adjusting on a changed view is possible but adds cost
management.close: reverse the opening trade (buy back short, sell long) or let a profitable spread expire

greeks.theta: time decay works against the position
greeks.vega: slightly benefits from rising IV, effect small since both buying and selling

when_to_use: moderate directional view
reduce cost versus buying an outright option

rules.text: Enter as a single spread order at the calculated net debit or within an acceptable range; check max profit/loss versus the risk-reward goal first.
Use debit spreads only with a directional view, bullish for call spreads and bearish for put spreads.

mechanics.point: Both legs must share the expiration; close by doing the opposite of the opening trade.
Debit spread caps loss at the debit and profit at width minus debit, unlike credit spreads where max loss exceeds max profit.

terms.definition: Spread where purchased options cost more than sold ones, giving a net cash outlay.
Debit call spread for a moderate rise.
Debit put spread for a moderate decline.

concepts-defending-positions.summary: Tasty approach to losing premium-selling trades: close at a net loss of 2x credit received, or roll forward only for a credit, ideally 7-21 days before expiration; account size affects ability to keep rolling.

rules.text: Close a premium-selling trade for a net loss equal to 2x the credit received; this leaves room for recovery while capping further loss (collect $1.00, close when the option is worth $3.00).
Roll a losing trade forward in time only for a net credit, which improves breakeven and cost basis; paying to roll worsens both while opening a low-probability trade.
Strikes can be moved closer to the stock when rolling but must still bring a credit; with naked options this usually means rolling further out in time.
Roll roughly 7-21 days before expiration to avoid growing gamma and assignment risk.
Keep individual trade risk small relative to the account; small accounts cannot absorb prolonged rolling of losers as easily as large ones.

stats.label: Optimal loss close point from tastylive research
stats.conditions: Premium-selling trades, tested on historical data across 1x, 2x, 3x loss multiples

mechanics.point: A defensive roll of an OTM short option usually lands ITM at the same strike, a below-50% POP trade, and locks in the previous loss.
Best case for a rolled short premium trade is the option moving from ITM back to OTM, erasing earlier losses and keeping the credits.

concepts-defending-positions.quote: a net loss of 2x credit received can be optimal

concepts-delta-neutral-hedging.summary: Delta-neutral hedging offsets an option position's directional exposure, usually with shares sized by a hedge ratio, so profit comes from volatility or time decay; it needs regular rebalancing and adds transaction costs.

rules.text: Accept a delta band rather than exactly zero, and rebalance periodically (daily, weekly or monthly depending on approach) by trading shares or adjusting strikes/expirations.
Frequent adjustments raise transaction costs; balancing with calls and puts can add unwanted vega or theta exposure.
Best suited to range-bound or volatile markets with no clear trend, and to traders targeting volatility or time decay rather than direction.

mechanics.point: Hedge ratio = option delta x number of contracts x 100 shares; e.g. 0.40 delta x 10 short calls = 400 shares to buy.
Positive delta (long stock, long calls) is offset with negative delta (short stock, long puts) and vice versa; example: 10 long puts at -0.30 delta = -300 delta, offset by buying 300 shares.
Hedging is mostly applied to single positions but can be done across a portfolio; it is not itself a profit source but shapes risk toward vol or theta goals.
Neutral delta shifts the profit focus to vega and theta.

terms.definition: Position whose net delta is near zero so small price moves barely change its value.
Number of shares needed to offset an options position's delta.
Re-adjusting the hedge as delta drifts.

concepts-delta.summary: Delta measures an option's price change per $1 move in the underlying; covers the other Greeks, delta by call/put and long/short, delta neutral hedge ratio, and delta as a rough ITM probability.

rules.text: Delta is a risk measure, not good or bad; use it to see directional exposure of a position or portfolio.
Delta neutral hedging uses shares sized by contracts x delta x multiplier to mute direction and isolate volatility.

numbers.name: example hedge shares for 100 contracts at 0.40 delta

mechanics.point: Call deltas range 0 to 1, put deltas -1 to 0; ATM is about 0.50 / -0.50. Near expiration ITM deltas drift toward 1 / -1 and OTM deltas toward 0. Delta is dynamic.
Gamma is the change in delta per $1 move; theta is value lost per day; vega is value change per 1% volatility move (higher for longer-dated and ATM options); rho is value change per 1% rate move.
Long calls and short puts are positive delta; short calls and long puts are negative delta. Delta works the same for long and short, only the P&L sign flips.
Delta is used loosely as the chance of finishing ITM (0.10 delta roughly 10%, 0.50 roughly 50%), but the page stresses it is only a rule of thumb, not a scientific estimate.

terms.definition: Expected option value change for a $1 move in the underlying.
Contracts x delta x multiplier gives shares needed to be delta neutral.
Position hedged to minimize directional exposure.

concepts-delta.quote: Delta is neither good nor bad

concepts-diagonal-spread.summary: Diagonal spread is a defined-risk directional debit trade: long ITM/ATM option in a farther expiration, short OTM option in a nearer one. Tastylive checks the short premium covers the long's extrinsic, caps debit at 75% of width, and closes at 25-50% of max profit.
unmapped: Diagonal vs vertical vs calendar comparison

strategy_notes.legs: Long call diagonal: buy ITM/ATM call in the later expiration, sell OTM call in the nearer expiration. Long put diagonal: buy ITM/ATM put in the later expiration, sell OTM put in the nearer expiration.
strategy_notes.max_profit: Roughly the strike distance between legs plus any extrinsic value left in the long option when the short expires, minus the debit; can exceed the spread width in value terms. Needs the spread to move fully ITM.
strategy_notes.max_loss: The debit paid, realized if the long option expires worthless.
strategy_notes.buying_power: Defined risk; risk equals the debit paid.

tasty_setup.strikes: Check the extrinsic value of the longer-dated ITM option; sell a near-term option whose premium is equal to or greater than that extrinsic. Deeper ITM long makes this easier.
tasty_setup.credit_target: Total debit no more than 75% of the strike width (page also says never pay more than the width).
tasty_setup.underlying: Never route diagonals in volatility instruments, since each expiration acts as its own underlying and max loss is not defined.

management.profit_target: Close at 25-50% of max profit; profit comes from the long moving further ITM and/or IV rising.
management.roll: Roll the short option down closer to the breakeven when the stock moves against the spread, collecting more premium; can also roll the short out in time toward the long expiration, or vertically toward the long strike.
management.defend: Manage when the stock moves against the spread by adjusting the short option; keep net debit below spread width after moving the short strike.
management.loss_rule: No stop given; trader decides whether to close for a loss or defend the long option.
management.close: Closing means trading the opposite of each leg held; can sell to close for less than max loss if the thesis changes.

greeks.theta: Short near-term option decays faster than the long, giving a temporary hedge.

when_to_use: Directional view with defined risk while aggressively lowering cost basis
Earnings: sell the inflated near-term IV and hold directional delta in a back month with less IV crush exposure, if directionally correct
when_to_avoid: Volatility instruments
Poor setup where short premium is smaller than long option extrinsic, which can lose money if the move comes too fast
mistakes: Paying a debit above the spread width
Ignoring that the short option hedge is only temporary

rules.text: Make sure the near-term short option's premium is at least equal to the extrinsic value of the long ITM option.
Keep the total debit at or under 75% of the strike width.

numbers.name: max debit as share of width

rules.text: Do not trade diagonal spreads in volatility products.
Close diagonals at 25-50% of max profit.
When the stock moves against the spread, roll the short option down toward breakeven to collect more premium and cut risk.

mechanics.point: Near-term earnings-cycle options hold most of their extrinsic as earnings premium; a later-cycle long option has a lower baseline IV and less exposure to the crush. Page example: 50 DTE expected move about +/-39.90 versus +/-19.41 for the 1 DTE cycle.
Because the short expires first, a new short can be sold against the remaining long to keep lowering cost basis.
Diagonals combine the vertical strike offset with a calendar-style expiration offset; compared with a calendar (same strike, cheaper, theta/IV driven), a diagonal is more directional.

terms.definition: Long and short options of the same type on different strikes and different expirations.
A vertical debit spread where the long leg has a later expiration than the short.

concepts-diagonal-spread.quote: Each expiration acts as its own underlying

concepts-dividend.summary: Explains dividends: regular vs special, the declaration, ex-dividend, record and payment dates, price drop on ex-date, and common dividend strategies (capture, high yield, growth, DRIP) with their risks.

mechanics.point: Stock typically drops by about the dividend amount on the ex-dividend date. Ex-date is the first day the stock trades without the dividend, set by the exchange, usually one business day (up to three) before the record date; buyers on or after it do not get the dividend.
Declaration date announces amount, record date and payment date; payment can come weeks after the record date.
Dividend capture risk: the ex-date price drop can exceed the dividend received, producing a net loss.

terms.definition: One-time payout outside the regular schedule, often from excess cash.
Annual dividends per share divided by current share price.
First day shares trade without entitlement to the upcoming dividend.

concepts-earnings.summary: Implied volatility rises into earnings and drops sharply afterward, so tastylive sticks to premium selling to capture the IV crush rather than trading direction, which is hard to predict.

rules.text: Sell premium before the earnings announcement and buy it back afterward to harvest the IV crush, especially if the stock barely moves.
Avoid directional earnings bets; stocks can fall on beats and rise on misses, so trade the volatility aspect instead.

mechanics.point: IV builds into earnings from speculation and hedging demand and falls quickly after the news; the whole curve can rise, with the nearest expirations moving by the largest percentages.

terms.definition: Usually quarterly public report of company earnings, quantified as earnings per share.

concepts-extrinsic-value.summary: Extrinsic (time) value is the option premium beyond intrinsic value. It is largest ATM, grows with time and implied volatility, shrinks with time decay, and is affected by rates and dividends.

mechanics.point: Extrinsic = option price minus intrinsic value. OTM options are entirely extrinsic; ITM options still carry some.
Extrinsic value is highest ATM and falls toward zero with time; deep ITM and OTM options lose it first while ATM holds it longest.
Higher implied volatility and more time to expiration both mean more extrinsic value.
Higher rates generally raise call extrinsic and lower put extrinsic; expected dividends do the reverse.

terms.definition: Amount an option is in the money; zero for OTM.
Part of premium beyond intrinsic value, also called time value.

concepts-futures-options.summary: Explains options on futures: contract rights and obligations, buyer versus seller risk, pros and cons, how they differ from futures, common uses, and why traders pick them over stock options.

rules.text: Selling futures options naked carries large risk; have a risk management plan before writing them.
Illiquid futures options make it hard to enter or exit at good prices; check liquidity first.
Mini, micro and small futures options let traders participate with less capital.

mechanics.point: Exercising a futures call gives a long position in the futures contract at the strike; exercising a futures put gives a short position. Different expirations can point to different underlying futures contracts.
Futures need a margin deposit rather than a premium; futures are marked to market daily while options are not.
Buyers risk only the premium. Short calls on futures have unlimited risk; short puts risk the strike value times contract size less premium, since price cannot go below zero.
Reasons to trade futures options over stock options: broad index or commodity exposure, leverage, near 24-hour trading, diversification, and potentially better liquidity and tighter spreads.
Costs include commissions, bid-ask spreads and premium paid.

terms.definition: Right, not obligation, to enter a specific futures contract at a set strike on or before expiration.
Daily crediting or debiting of futures gains and losses to the account.

concepts-gamma.summary: Gamma is how much an option's delta shifts per $1 move in the underlying; long options have positive gamma, short options negative; gamma is highest near the money and rises toward expiration; gamma hedging means maintaining delta hedges.

rules.text: Traders who want to avoid gamma risk can close positions well ahead of expiration, since gamma climbs as expiry nears.

Two management philosophies: manage winners and losers by P/L mechanically, or manage early by closing after a set number of days or a set number of days before expiration, because P/L per day falls as expiration approaches.
Gamma risk can also be reduced with delta and gamma hedging, usually paired with a volatility-based delta-neutral approach rather than used alone.

stats.label: Rule-of-thumb high gamma level
stats.conditions: Page calls this a general guideline for relatively high gamma

mechanics.point: Gamma equals the change in delta divided by the change in underlying price; its value runs from 0 to 1.

Long options: gamma adds to delta when the stock rises and subtracts when it falls (positive gamma). Short options: the reverse (negative gamma). Example: long call delta 0.40, gamma 0.10 goes to 0.50 on +$1 and 0.30 on -$1; short call delta -0.25, gamma 0.05 goes to -0.30 on +$1 and -0.20 on -$1.
Gamma is larger for ATM and ITM options than OTM, and increases as expiration approaches; higher gamma means delta changes faster.
Gamma is neither good nor bad; it is a risk measure for position or portfolio.
Delta hedging (e.g. shorting stock against a long call) isolates the volatility edge, and the ongoing re-adjustment of that hedge as price moves is called gamma hedging.

terms.definition: Rate of change of an option's delta per $1 move in the underlying.
Long option exposure where delta moves in favor of the holder as price moves.
Short option exposure where delta moves against the seller as price moves.
Repeatedly adjusting stock hedges to keep a delta-neutral position.

concepts-hedging.summary: Overview of hedging: offsetting risk with options, futures, forwards or swaps; steps, reasons, pros and cons, hedge types (short/long futures hedges, protective put, covered call, forwards), a protective put example, and the risks of imperfect or costly hedges.

strategy_notes.legs: own shares plus buy a put on the same stock (example: 100 shares at $50, buy a 3-month $45 put for $3)
strategy_notes.outlook: long-term bullish but worried about a near-term drop
strategy_notes.max_profit: Unlimited upside from the stock, reduced by the premium paid
strategy_notes.max_loss: Limited: stock decline down to the strike plus premium (example sells effectively at $42 net)
when_to_use: Want to keep the shares but guard against a drop, especially in volatile markets
when_to_avoid: Highly risk-tolerant investors chasing returns, since premium drags performance
mistakes: Wrong timing, wrong instrument or wrong hedge size

rules.text: Hedging steps: identify the risk, choose the instrument, implement, then monitor and adjust or close the hedge if the risk fades.
Run scenario analysis across many outcomes to confirm a hedge matches outlook, goals and risk profile before placing it.
Hedging suits risk-averse investors and high-volatility periods; it fits less well for risk-tolerant investors who want maximum returns.
Weigh hedge costs (premium, transaction costs) against benefits, since they can outweigh protection and cap upside.

mechanics.point: An ideal hedge gains when the core position loses; it can still lose money or offset gains when the market moves favorably.
A covered call gives income and some downside cushion but caps upside above the strike.
Illiquid hedging instruments can make setup or unwinding difficult.

terms.definition: A position taken to offset or reduce risk in another position or portfolio.
A hedge whose price moves do not fully offset the risk being hedged.
Selling futures to lock in a sale price for an asset you own.
Buying futures to lock in a purchase price for an asset you plan to buy.

concepts-how-are-options-taxed.summary: US tax overview for options: equity options taxed by holding period with short premium always short-term, index/non-equity Section 1256 60/40 treatment, and wash sale rule applying to options.

rules.text: Be careful with wash sales: a loss sale followed by repurchase of a substantially identical option or stock within 30 days may disallow the loss.
Consult a tax professional since treatment varies with option type, holding period and changing law.

stats.label: Section 1256 treatment split
stats.conditions: applies to index and other non-equity options regardless of holding period

mechanics.point: Long equity options held under a year give short-term gains or losses (ordinary rates); held over a year can qualify as long-term.
Premium from selling/writing an option is generally short-term, and gains or losses on short options are short-term regardless of how long the position was open.
Calls and puts are taxed the same; what matters is long versus short and the holding period.
Non-equity options such as index or commodity options often fall under Section 1256 and the 60/40 rule, which may lower tax for active traders.
Wash sale disallowed loss is added to the cost basis of the replacement and deferred; options can be treated as substantially identical to the stock, so mixed stock/option trades matter.

terms.definition: Non-equity option category with blended 60/40 long/short-term tax treatment.
Loss disallowed when the same or substantially identical security is bought within 30 days before or after the sale.

concepts-how-to-pick-the-right-strike-pr.summary: Generic framework for choosing strike and expiration: tie them to outlook, risk tolerance, volatility, Greeks and time horizon, and compare alternatives by scenario analysis, illustrated with covered call and put credit spread strike pairs.

strategy_notes.legs: own 100 shares, sell 1 call; example compares a closer strike with a higher premium against a farther strike with a lower premium
strategy_notes.max_profit: Premium received if shares stay below the strike (page example, generic prices)
strategy_notes.max_loss: Page computes it as strike minus purchase price plus premium, per share; farther strike gives a larger figure in its example
when_to_use: Investor holds shares and wants premium income while accepting a capped upside

strategy_notes.legs: sell higher-strike put, buy lower-strike put, same expiration; two example width/strike placements compared
strategy_notes.max_profit: Net credit received
strategy_notes.max_loss: Spread width minus net credit
when_to_use: Slightly bullish view; both options expire worthless if the stock stays above the short strike

rules.text: Choose strikes from outlook, risk tolerance, current volatility and trend, Greeks and time horizon rather than in isolation.
Elevated volatility may justify wider strike selection; a rangebound market may favor narrower placement.
Conservative traders lean toward near- or at-the-money strikes; those seeking higher returns may use OTM strikes with lower cost but higher risk.
Pick expiration together with strike: a near-term expected move suits a short-dated ATM strike, a gradual multi-month view suits longer-dated options.
Compare candidate strike combinations through scenario analysis of max gain, max loss and preferred outcome before entering.

mechanics.point: ATM options cost more than OTM because they are more likely to finish ITM.
Shorter expiration means faster time decay; longer expiration costs more premium and gives the move more time to play out.
Higher implied volatility raises premiums, and longer expirations usually embed more expected volatility and higher premium.
In a vertical credit spread the max loss equals width minus credit, and a wider or farther-OTM structure changes the credit/risk trade-off.

terms.definition: The fixed price at which an option holder may buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying.
Classification of an option as ITM, ATM or OTM based on strike versus underlying price.

concepts-how-to-start-trading-options-en.summary: A nine-step entry checklist for options: market assumption, liquidity, IV, IV rank, strategy, strikes, expiry, position sizing and rules-based management, stressing a mechanical, probability-driven process.

rules.text: Start with a market assumption built from technicals, fundamentals or macro events.
Favor options with high volume and open interest; illiquid ones mean wider spreads and higher costs.
High IV rank (current IV vs roughly the past 52 weeks) points toward selling premium; low IV rank points toward buying options.
Match strategy to assumption and vol environment, e.g. bearish on volatility in high IV suggests selling options.
Pick expiry by how long the thesis needs: longer costs more premium, short-term events suit shorter expiries.
Size each trade so it cannot cause outsized portfolio damage; riskier trades get smaller size.
Use rules-based management: manage winners and losers by P&L targets or manage early by time, to avoid emotional decisions.

mechanics.point: IV often overestimates future realized movement, so reading IV helps judge whether options are rich or cheap.
IV rank compares today's implied volatility to its own range, usually over the last 52 weeks.

terms.definition: A hypothesis about how an asset or market will behave, used to direct the trade.
Closing positions when remaining risk outweighs remaining reward, based on time.

concepts-how-to-trade-0dte-options.summary: Beginner overview of 0DTE options: what they are, strategies suited to them, steps to trade them, and risks such as gaps, IV sensitivity, illiquidity and costs. No tastylive numeric rules.

strategy_notes.legs: any standard structure applied on the final day: naked options, covered calls, cash-secured puts, verticals, iron condors, straddles/strangles
strategy_notes.risk: varies; naked shorts carry unlimited risk

tasty_setup.underlying: almost any optionable stock/ETF on its last day; SPY and QQQ list explicit 0DTE

when_to_use: want to profit from a sharp move or from rapid premium collapse at expiration
when_to_avoid: overleveraging, especially when selling
low-liquidity names
mistakes: ignoring wider bid-asks and slippage
too little time to adjust

rules.text: Size positions from risk per trade, capital and desired reward/risk; avoid overleveraging short 0DTE options.
Expect wider spreads and slippage in illiquid short-dated options.
Have a predefined exit plan using a price target, indicator, or market shift.

stats.label: Share of equity options volume with under 5 days to expiration

mechanics.point: Orders can be market, limit or stop; the brokerage must allow options trading.
Frequent short-term trading raises commissions and slippage.

terms.definition: Option on its last trading session.

concepts-how-to-trade-earnings-with-opti.summary: Overview of trading earnings with options: IV inflates into the report and crushes after, with long and short straddles/strangles, long calendars and covered calls as common structures, plus preparation tips.

strategy_notes.legs: buy call and put, same expiration, same strike (strangle uses different strikes)
strategy_notes.outlook: volatility up; expect a bigger move than priced, direction unknown
when_to_use: expect stock to move more than the market anticipates

strategy_notes.legs: sell call and put, same expiration, same strike (strangle uses different strikes)
strategy_notes.outlook: volatility down; stock moves less than expected

tasty_setup.iv: inflated pre-earnings IV

strategy_notes.outlook: stock stays near strike; benefits from vol crush
when_to_use: profit from post-earnings volatility crush with stock near strike

strategy_notes.outlook: sideways to slightly higher after earnings
when_to_use: extra income if stock trades sideways or up slightly
cushion in a selloff

rules.text: Because earnings can bring large moves, consider scaling back and trading smaller.

Calls have intrinsic value when the strike is below the stock price; puts when the strike is above it. OTM options are all extrinsic.
Extrinsic value is largest ATM and tapers off further OTM and ITM (bell-shaped without skew); more time means more extrinsic value, and it decays as expiration nears (theta decay).
Higher IV, meaning greater perceived uncertainty about future movement, raises extrinsic value; lower IV lowers it. IV is derived from current option prices.
On expiration day options trade close to intrinsic value because little time remains for the stock to move.

terms.definition: The amount an ITM option would be worth if exercised now: distance between strike and stock price.
The part of the premium above intrinsic value, reflecting time and implied volatility.
The daily erosion of an option's extrinsic value as expiration approaches.
The market's expectation of how far the underlying may move over a year, inferred from option prices.

concepts-options-expiration.summary: Expiration cycles (weekly, monthly, LEAPS, 0DTE), expiration timing, what happens at expiry ITM/OTM/partially ITM spreads, DNE requests, and tastylive's 45 DTE finding for short options.

rules.text: Research on short options found a 45-day duration balances accelerating extrinsic decay with enough distance from the stock price to collect premium at entry.
Close narrow or ATM spreads just before expiration to avoid one leg being exercised and the other expiring worthless, which can turn small defined risk into large share risk.
Know the exact expiration date and time of a product before opening a position.

mechanics.point: US monthly equity options expire the third Friday at 3:00 p.m. CST, moving to the prior Thursday if that Friday is a holiday; LEAPS (over one year) follow the same rule.

Weeklies are the same as monthlies but shorter; typically listed on Thursday and expire eight days later, with up to five weekly expirations available; monthlies are listed roughly 1 to 11 months out.
SPY and SPX-type products list expirations every trading day (0DTE).
ITM options at expiry convert automatically to 100 shares per contract: long call long stock, short call short stock, long put short stock, short put long stock.
OTM options expire worthless and vanish from the account.
Cash-settled products like SPX have no shares, so ITM options settle to cash; SPX monthlies are AM-settled (last trade Thursday), while SPX weeklies are PM-settled at 3pm CST.
To avoid exercise of a long ITM option, submit a Do Not Exercise request to the broker promptly after the close on expiration day; cutoffs vary by broker.

terms.definition: The nearest regular monthly expiration; also called near or spot month.
Options with more than a year until expiration.
Do Not Exercise request sent to the broker for a long ITM option.

concepts-options-leverage.summary: Explains how the 100-share multiplier lets options control large exposure with small capital, how to compute a leverage ratio, and how leverage differs for long versus short options.

rules.text: Because leverage magnifies losses, plan worst cases and use risk controls such as stop-loss levels, especially with short options.
Uncovered short calls carry theoretically unlimited loss; short puts risk the stock going to zero.

mechanics.point: Equity option multiplier is 100 shares per contract, so a small premium controls a large notional position.
Leverage ratio is stock position value divided by option cost; the page example is a 10,000 stock position versus a 200 call, giving 50:1.
For short options, leverage can be gauged against buying power required; margin and portfolio margin accounts allow selling without posting the full true risk.
Long options lose at most the premium (possibly 100%); short options can lose far more than the credit, particularly on gap moves.

terms.definition: Value of the underlying exposure divided by the capital outlay for the option.
Shares controlled per contract, normally 100 for equity options.

concepts-options-liquidity.summary: Options liquidity explained via bid-ask spread, open interest, volume, depth and immediacy; why wide spreads raise costs and risk, and how an illiquid strike differs from an illiquid symbol.

rules.text: Judge liquidity using bid-ask width, open interest and volume together, plus depth and fill speed; check at contract, symbol and market level.
Avoid illiquid symbols and strikes; multi-leg strategies especially need contracts across several strikes and expirations.
Expect wider spreads during volatile markets even in liquid underlyings.

stats.label: Round-trip cost illustration
stats.conditions: buy at $1.00 ask, sell at $0.50 bid on a 50-cent wide market versus a penny-wide $0.99/$1.00 market

mechanics.point: Open interest is cumulative outstanding contracts while volume resets daily; low open interest with low volume signals illiquidity.
A single illiquid strike can be handled by shifting strikes or expirations; an illiquid symbol cannot.
Wide bid-ask spreads force worse fills, raising transaction costs and hurting short-term strategies most.

terms.definition: Gap between best buyer price and best seller price; narrow means liquid.
Number of outstanding contracts not yet closed, exercised or expired.

concepts-options-premium.summary: Option premium equals intrinsic plus extrinsic value, driven by underlying price, time, implied volatility and rates; extrinsic value decays to zero by expiry, vol crush cuts premium, and IV Rank helps judge whether premium is cheap or expensive.

rules.text: Use IV Rank to judge premium richness; a high IV Rank implies expensive premium and can favor selling options, a low rank means cheap premium.
Buying options at inflated premium before a known event risks losses from vol crush even if the stock does not move; OTM options are most exposed since they are all extrinsic value.
Short premium can gain from vol crush, but a large adverse underlying move can outweigh that benefit.

mechanics.point: Premium = intrinsic value + extrinsic value; quotes are per share so a $1.00 quote is $100 per contract.
Extrinsic value decays to zero at expiration and decay accelerates near expiry; only intrinsic value remains if ITM.
Higher implied volatility raises premium; higher rates modestly raise call and lower put premiums.
IV Rank places current IV within its range over a period, usually the past year; an example 80% rank means IV is above 80% of that period's levels.
After events like earnings, IV can drop sharply and premium falls even with an unchanged stock price.

terms.definition: The actual market price paid by the buyer and received by the seller of an option.
The in-the-money amount an option would be worth if exercised now.
Time and volatility based part of premium that decays to zero by expiry.
Current implied volatility placed within its high-low range over a lookback, shown as a percentage.

concepts-order-types.summary: Explains the main order types (limit, market, stop-loss, stop-limit, trailing stop) and time-in-force options (day, GTC, IOC, FOK, AON), with fill and risk tradeoffs.

rules.text: Use a limit order when price control matters more than certainty of fill; a market order when speed matters, accepting a variable fill.
Stop-loss converts to a market order when triggered (guaranteed execution, uncertain price); stop-limit converts to a limit (price guaranteed, fill not).
Set stop levels wide enough for normal fluctuation, wider for volatile stocks, and review them regularly.

numbers.name: example stop distance below purchase (5% or 10%)

mechanics.point: Buy limit fills at or below the limit, sell limit at or above; partial fills are possible; unfilled limit orders cancel at session end unless GTC.
Market order fills depend on volume and bid-ask spread; thin liquidity, large size or fast markets can fill far from the quote.
Time in force: GTC lasts until filled, expired or cancelled (broker caps duration); IOC fills what it can immediately and cancels the rest; FOK is all immediately or nothing; AON requires full size.
Stop orders trigger at-or-through the stop price; buy stops sit above market, sell stops below; gaps can cause fills far from the stop.

terms.definition: A stop whose trigger follows the market at a fixed percent or point distance.
Order that persists until filled, expired or cancelled.

concepts-pattern-day-trader-pdt-rule.summary: Explains the FINRA pattern day trader rule: four or more day trades in a rolling five-day window in a margin account triggers a $25,000 minimum equity requirement, day trade margin calls, and the general risks of day trading.

rules.text: A margin account that makes four or more day trades inside a rolling five-day period is classed as a pattern day trader and must hold at least $25,000 in the account.
If a pattern day trader's balance drops under the minimum, further day trades are restricted until the account is refunded.
Respond to a day trade call by depositing funds; the page gives a window of about five business days as an example before restriction.
Avoid overtrading and emotional decisions in an attempt to recover losses; follow a risk plan.

mechanics.point: The PDT rule is enforced under FINRA and applies to margin accounts; fewer than four day trades in five days does not trigger the $25,000 requirement.
Non-PDT customers follow their broker's own margin requirements, which vary by broker and security type.
Starting day trading buying power is the account's maintenance excess from the prior day's close.
Leverage in margin accounts can magnify losses beyond the original position value and cause margin calls.

terms.definition: A margin account holder with four or more day trades in a rolling five-day period.
Notice that a PDT account is below the $25,000 minimum and needs funding.

concepts-poor-man-covered-call.summary: PMCC is a long call diagonal that mimics a covered call using a deep ITM back-month call instead of shares; page covers structure, max profit/loss formulas, assignment handling, and tastylive setup checks (extrinsic coverage, debit cap).

strategy_notes.legs: buy deep ITM back-month call (several months to years out, e.g. a LEAP, high delta) and sell a shorter-term OTM call on the same stock
strategy_notes.max_profit: Approximately width of call strikes minus net debit paid; exact figure cannot be computed because expirations differ. Realized if stock is at the short strike at short-call expiration.
strategy_notes.max_loss: Cost of the long call minus premium received from the short call (long call goes to zero)
strategy_notes.breakevens: Approximately long call strike plus net debit paid

tasty_setup.dte: short call typically 30 to 60 days out; long call several months to years
tasty_setup.strikes: long call deep ITM with high delta; short call OTM
tasty_setup.iv: page lists low IV as the ideal environment
tasty_setup.credit_target: Total debit should not exceed 75% of the strike width; short call premium should be at least the extrinsic value of the long call
tasty_setup.underlying: never in volatility instruments, because each expiration acts as its own underlying and max loss is not defined

management.roll: On a losing trade where the stock fell, roll the short call to a lower strike for more credit. Near short expiry, let it expire, buy it back, or roll later or to another strike.
management.close: Best case: stock rises sharply in one cycle, options trade near intrinsic value and remaining profit potential shrinks, so close as a winner
management.assignment: If short call is assigned, either exercise the deep ITM long call to get shares that offset the short stock, or buy shares in the market and sell the long call

strategy_notes.accounts: Useful in smaller accounts to replicate a covered call with far less capital and risk
when_to_use: Moderately bullish or neutral long-term view on a stock or ETF
Want covered-call-like income with less capital
Smaller accounts
when_to_avoid: Volatility instruments
Setups where the short call premium is below the long call extrinsic value or debit exceeds 75% of width
mistakes: A poor setup can lose money even if the stock moves in your favor too fast
Ignoring early assignment risk when the short call goes ITM, especially around dividends
Giving up gains above the short strike

rules.text: Check the extrinsic value of the long ITM call and make sure the short call sold is worth at least that much; deeper ITM long calls make this easier.
Keep the total debit paid at or below 75% of the strike width.

numbers.name: max debit as share of width

rules.text: Do not trade PMCCs in volatility instruments; max loss becomes undefined.
Short call is typically 30 to 60 days out and OTM; long call is deep ITM with a long expiration and high delta.
When the stock drops, roll the short call to a lower strike to collect more credit.
Close for a win after a big one-cycle rally since options then trade near intrinsic and little profit remains.

mechanics.point: Early assignment of the short call is possible once ITM (American style, dividends can trigger it). Since no shares are owned, you resolve it by exercising the long call or buying shares and selling the long call.
Max profit and breakeven are only estimates because the two legs expire in different cycles.

terms.definition: Long call diagonal debit spread that stands in for a covered call using a long-dated call instead of shares.
Long-dated option, often deep ITM, used as the stock substitute.

concepts-poor-man-covered-put.summary: Poor man's covered put: long-dated ATM/ITM put (often LEAPS) paired with a near-term OTM short put, a defined-risk lower-capital stand-in for a covered put, usable bearish or sideways.

strategy_notes.legs: buy long-dated ATM or ITM put (LEAPS-style), sell near-term OTM put with a lower strike
strategy_notes.max_profit: not fixed; depends on remaining extrinsic in the long put at short expiry; estimated as strike width minus net debit plus remaining extrinsic
strategy_notes.max_loss: initial net debit (long put cost minus short put credit), e.g. both puts worthless if stock rises
strategy_notes.breakevens: estimate: long put strike minus net debit (exact value not computable due to differing expirations)
strategy_notes.buying_power: lower capital than a traditional covered put, which needs short stock and large margin; cost is the net debit

tasty_setup.dte: short put near-term, long put long-dated
tasty_setup.strikes: long put strike above the short put strike
tasty_setup.iv: low IV is ideal environment

management.roll: roll the short put out in time, possibly new strike, for more premium or to change view
management.loss_rule: set stop-loss levels or close conditions in advance
management.close: buy back short put when it loses value, then optionally sell another near-term put; or close both legs together to avoid a leftover naked leg
management.assignment: if stock falls below short strike, short put may be exercised but the long put covers downside

greeks.theta: long put decays slowly and is a wasting asset in sideways markets

when_to_use: bearish outlook wanting capital efficiency vs shorting stock
moderately flat market, selling successive near-term puts against the long put
mistakes: ignoring time decay on the long put
closing only one leg and leaving a naked option

rules.text: Know max loss up front and plan exit conditions; watch the underlying and adjust if outlook changes.
Most spreads are closed with both legs at once to avoid leaving a naked option.

mechanics.point: Traditional covered put needs short stock and substantial margin with unlimited upside risk; the poor man's version replaces short stock with a long put so capital need is the net debit.

terms.definition: Long-dated put used instead of short stock, paired with a near-term short put for income.
The long-dated put against which short-term puts are repeatedly sold.

concepts-positive-correlation.summary: Defines correlation as a coefficient from -1 to +1; positive means assets move together. Describes strength labels and gives gold and silver as a strong example. Correlation is neutral, neither good nor bad.

stats.label: Long-term average correlation between gold and silver

mechanics.point: Positive correlation runs 0 to +1, negative -1 to 0; values like 0.15 are weak and 0.90 strong; a perfect +1 is rare in real markets.

terms.definition: Statistic from -1 to +1 showing how closely two assets' prices move together.
A coefficient of exactly +1.

concepts-probability-of-profit.summary: POP is the chance of making at least a penny; selling options and cost-basis reduction raise it above a coin flip, while buying spreads aims for roughly 50% by placing breakeven near the current price.

rules.text: When buying options, use spreads (not naked longs) and aim for breakeven at or slightly better than the current stock price.
Selling ATM or OTM options and collecting credit improves breakeven and POP.
Selling one call per 100 shares reduces cost basis and lifts a coin-flip stock position to higher POP.

stats.label: POP when buying spreads with breakeven near current price

mechanics.point: Breakeven distance drives POP; credits shift breakeven in the seller's favor.

terms.definition: Probability of making at least $0.01 on a trade.

concepts-protective-put.summary: Explains the protective put: buying puts against shares you own as downside insurance, with premium cost reducing upside, contract-count sizing, expiration choice, rolling, and worked up/down examples.

strategy_notes.legs: own shares (typically 100 per contract) and buy a put on the same underlying
strategy_notes.outlook: bullish long-term holding, worried about downside
strategy_notes.max_profit: unlimited stock upside minus the premium paid

tasty_setup.dte: longer expirations give more time but cost higher premium; duration is a key trade-off
tasty_setup.strikes: strike sets the floor price where shares can be sold
tasty_setup.underlying: shares already held or newly bought

management.roll: Roll by selling the near put and buying a later-dated one at once, or buy a new put after expiry; rolling keeps continuous protection.
management.assignment: If shares fall below the strike, the put can be exercised to sell at the strike.

when_to_use: uncertainty or concern about a significant drop while wanting to keep upside
alternative to selling the position outright
when_to_avoid: when repeated premium cost would exceed benefit if the stock does not fall
mistakes: letting the put expire and being unprotected if the stock then drops
ignoring that cumulative premium can outweigh protection

rules.text: One put contract covers 100 shares, so 200 shares need two puts for full protection; hedging a portion (one put) saves premium.
To keep protection going, roll the put to a later expiration (sell old, buy new) or buy a new put after expiry.
Choose put expiration carefully: longer dated puts give time but cost more premium.

mechanics.point: Example: 100 shares at $50 with a $50 put bought for $2. If stock falls to $40 net loss is $200 instead of $1,000; if it rises to $60 net gain is $800 instead of $1,000.

terms.definition: A put bought against owned shares to set a floor on the sale price.
Replacing an expiring put with a later-dated one to maintain coverage.

concepts-put-call-parity.summary: Put-call parity ties call, put, stock and strike prices together (call minus put equals stock minus strike), with a dividend adjustment; discrepancies may reflect dividends, volatility or liquidity, and American options add early exercise complexity.

rules.text: If a parity gap cannot be explained, consider avoiding those options.

mechanics.point: Parity formula: call - put = stock - strike; with dividends, call = stock - strike + put - dividend (page's simplified form).
American options may be exercised early near dividends, complicating the relationship.
Worked example: stock 30.50 and a 30 put at 1.10 imply a 1.60 call; with a 0.30 dividend, 1.30.

terms.definition: Pricing link between same-strike, same-expiry calls and puts and the stock.

concepts-put-options.summary: Introduces put options: the long put as a bearish, defined-risk bet, the short put as neutral-to-bullish premium collection with assignment risk, ways to close a long put, and comparisons with calls and short stock.

strategy_notes.legs: buy one put option (right to sell 100 shares at the strike)
strategy_notes.max_loss: the premium (debit) paid up front, 100% of it if the put expires worthless
strategy_notes.breakevens: strike minus the debit paid

tasty_setup.iv: some traders buy puts or put spreads when IV rank is low, so less extrinsic value is paid

management.close: Three ways to close: let it expire worthless, sell it before expiration, or exercise into 100 short shares (rare except for ITM options with little extrinsic value).
management.assignment: Puts that are $0.01 ITM at expiration are typically exercised automatically, leaving the owner short 100 shares.

greeks.theta: extrinsic value decays to zero by expiration
greeks.vega: gains when IV rises, which often happens as the stock drops

when_to_use: expecting a significant near-term drop in the underlying
wanting short exposure with capped loss instead of shorting shares
when_to_avoid: when the stock is expected to stay above the strike
mistakes: holding an OTM put to expiration and losing all extrinsic value

strategy_notes.legs: sell one put option, obligation to buy 100 shares at the strike if assigned
strategy_notes.max_profit: the credit received up front

management.assignment: If assigned the seller is put 100 shares; many traders sell puts deliberately to acquire shares at a lower cost basis than the current market, keeping the premium.

greeks.theta: profits as time passes

when_to_use: bullish or neutral view, willing to own shares at the strike
when_to_avoid: when uncomfortable holding 100 shares of risk below the strike
mistakes: forgetting profit is capped at the credit on a big rally, unlike owning stock

rules.text: Some traders place long puts or long put spreads when IV rank is low, because the extrinsic value paid is smaller.
A long put can be closed by selling it before expiration, which keeps any remaining extrinsic value; exercising is uncommon.
Only sell a put if comfortable with the risk of owning 100 shares below the strike, less the premium collected.

mechanics.point: A long put owner can exercise to short 100 shares; the put seller is then assigned and must buy 100 shares at the strike.
Puts that finish at least $0.01 in the money at expiration are typically exercised automatically.
Put value rises when the stock falls and often when IV rises (IV commonly increases as stocks drop); extrinsic value always decays to zero by expiration.
Buying a put needs no stock ownership; max loss is the debit, versus undefined loss on shorting stock outright.

terms.definition: A contract giving the owner the right to sell 100 shares at the strike by expiration.
The amount paid per contract to own the option.
The seller's obligation to fulfill the contract when the owner exercises.

concepts-ratio-spread.summary: Front ratio spreads (long vertical plus an extra short at the short strike, entered for a credit) remove risk on one side, peak at the short strike, and carry undefined risk beyond breakeven; back ratios (ZEBRA) are debit stock replacements.

strategy_notes.legs: Front ratio: buy one ATM/OTM call (or put) and sell two further-OTM options of the same type, same expiration, so the whole trade is a net credit. Back ratio is the inverse: more long than short, entered for a debit.
strategy_notes.outlook: Put front ratio neutral-bearish (long delta start, no upside risk); call front ratio neutral-bullish (short delta start, no downside risk). Described as omni-directional when done for a credit.
strategy_notes.max_profit: Width of the embedded vertical plus the credit received; reached only if the underlying pins at the short strike at expiration. If the risk-free side is where price goes, you keep the credit.
strategy_notes.max_loss: Undefined past breakeven on the side with the extra short option; no risk on the other side when done for a credit.
strategy_notes.breakevens: Put: short put strike minus max profit potential. Call: short call strike plus max profit potential. Wider embedded spread gives a better breakeven.

tasty_setup.strikes: Place the short strike at the price target for the underlying, since that yields max profit at expiration.
tasty_setup.iv: High IV preferred: more extrinsic in far OTM strikes lets you widen the embedded spread and still collect a credit.
tasty_setup.credit_target: Route for a net credit so the OTM side has no risk; the credit is the profit if the spread expires OTM.
tasty_setup.underlying: Put-skewed products make put front ratios wider/better than calls.

management.profit_target: Close at 25% to 50% of max profit potential.
management.roll: Roll the whole spread out; or roll only the naked short option and sell the long spread near max value to lock in cost-basis reduction; can roll the extra short to the next month to extend duration.
management.defend: When the debit spread portion can be closed near max value, sell it and keep the extra short option; roll that short out if more duration is wanted.
management.close: 25-50% of max profit.
management.assignment: If assigned on the extra short call, convert to covered put (sell a put after); if assigned on the extra short put, convert to covered call.

greeks.delta: Put front ratio starts long delta; call front ratio starts short delta.

when_to_use: Have a price target for the underlying and want to enter a long or short stock-like position with a favorable breakeven
High IV environment
Put-skewed underlying for put ratios, since the skewed side allows a wider spread for the same credit
when_to_avoid: Low IV, where the embedded spread must be very narrow to still get a credit
Back ratios are normally not routed by tastylive because they are debits
mistakes: Assuming high POP means high chance of max profit; max profit needs a pin at the short strike
Ignoring the price level the underlying must not breach, since risk is undefined

strategy_notes.legs: Back ratio spread / ZEBRA: buy two ITM options and sell one ATM option so extrinsic value is about zero.
strategy_notes.outlook: Call version neutral-bullish (big up move benefits); put version bearish.
strategy_notes.max_profit: Call version unlimited; estimated as distance from long ITM strike to stock price minus the debit. Put version profit from large selloff.
strategy_notes.max_loss: The debit paid, realized if the spread is OTM at expiration.
strategy_notes.breakevens: Brought to about the stock price (roughly 50/50 probability); put version: long strike minus debit.

tasty_setup.strikes: Two ITM longs, one ATM/OTM short to cancel extrinsic value.

greeks.delta: Near 100 delta for the call ZEBRA.

when_to_use: Stock replacement with a fraction of the risk of 100 shares
when_to_avoid: Not a high-probability trade

rules.text: Route front ratio spreads for a net credit so there is no risk on the OTM side.
Prefer high IV for ratio spreads; richer far-OTM premium allows a wider embedded spread and better breakeven.
Set the short strike at your price target for the underlying.
Place the short options on the skewed side to get a wider breakeven or more credit for the same distance.
Close the position at 25% to 50% of maximum profit.
If the long vertical can be sold near max value, sell it and keep the extra short, rolling it to the next month for more duration.
Management options without changing structure: roll the whole spread out, or roll only the naked short while selling the long spread near max value.
tastylive does not normally route back ratio spreads for debits; the front ratio is the go-to.

mechanics.point: Put skew makes equidistant OTM puts richer than calls, so call ratios must be narrower than put ratios to still collect a credit; skew arises from hedging demand for puts.
Front ratios have high POP due to one-sided risk removal and generous breakeven, but POP of max profit is low because a pin is required.
Assignment on the extra short option converts the trade into a covered put (calls) or covered call (puts).

terms.definition: Vertical spread with an extra short option at the short strike, making a net credit.
More long options than short, entered for a debit with unlimited profit on one side.
Zero extrinsic value back ratio: two ITM longs against one ATM short, a near-100-delta stock replacement.

concepts-risk-management.summary: General primer on trading risk types and generic risk controls: stops and take-profits, hedging, per-trade sizing (1% and 2% rules), diversification, leverage and dollar-cost averaging, with a share-sizing example and a put-hedge example.

rules.text: Risk no more than about 1% of the total portfolio on any single trade; this limits damage from a run of consecutive losers.
A more aggressive variant allows up to 2% risk per trade, suited to higher risk tolerance, at the cost of larger potential drawdowns.
Share count for a stop-based trade = dollar risk allowed divided by per-share loss to the stop (example: $500 risk / $10 stop distance = 50 shares).
In volatile markets, cutting position size back is an effective way to limit risk.
Stick to highly liquid underlyings to reduce liquidity risk, since illiquid assets may force a worse exit price.
Use predefined stop-loss and take-profit exits so decisions are not driven by emotion during swings.
Spread exposure across assets, sectors and regions that are not perfectly correlated to cut asset-specific risk; market-wide risk cannot be diversified away.
Keep borrowed leverage in line with account size and risk tolerance, because it magnifies both gains and losses (5:1 leverage turns a 5% move into about 25%).
Buying puts against a long stock holding offsets part of a decline at the cost of the premium; the cost is lost if the stock rises.

mechanics.point: Size from the loss you can tolerate: max loss budget (percent of account) divided by loss per unit at the stop gives the quantity.
Event risk and binary events (regulatory decisions, M&A, disasters) produce sharp unpredictable gaps that stops and diversification may not contain.
Systematic (market) risk persists regardless of diversification; unsystematic (single-company) risk shrinks as holdings spread out.
Leverage scales returns and losses proportionally to the leverage ratio.

terms.definition: Risk from market-wide forces that diversification cannot remove.
Risk specific to one company, sector or asset that diversification can reduce.
Risk of having to accept a poor price because an asset cannot be sold quickly.
Risk of sudden large price moves from unforeseeable occurrences, including binary outcomes.
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price.

concepts-short-call.summary: A short (naked) call collects premium and obliges the seller to deliver shares at the strike; profit is capped at the premium, loss is theoretically unlimited, so it suits experienced traders with a neutral-to-bearish view and close monitoring.

strategy_notes.legs: sell one call option, choosing a strike the underlying is not expected to exceed
strategy_notes.max_profit: Premium received, if the underlying stays below the strike and the call expires worthless
strategy_notes.max_loss: Theoretically unlimited as the underlying rises, less premium received

management.close: Needs close monitoring and quick action if price moves strongly against the position
management.assignment: If exercised, seller must sell the asset at the strike

greeks.theta: Time decay benefits the seller

when_to_use: Sideways or declining market where little movement is expected
Income generation in flat markets
when_to_avoid: Volatile or bullish markets
Without strong risk management or options-selling experience
mistakes: Holding without risk management
Being surprised by news-driven surges

rules.text: Short calls are for experienced traders confident the underlying will stay flat or fall; sharp rallies can produce large losses beyond the premium.
Monitor closely and be ready to act if the underlying moves well against the strike.

mechanics.point: If the buyer exercises, the seller must deliver at the strike regardless of how high the market price is; example: $55 strike, stock at $60, $3 premium gives a $2 per share net loss.
Position profits from time decay and a flat or falling underlying and gets no benefit from rising volatility.

terms.definition: Sold call option giving the seller an obligation to sell the underlying at the strike if exercised.

concepts-standard-deviation.summary: Standard deviation, read from implied volatility, gives the market's expected range; a 16% ITM strike marks one SD, about 2.5% marks two; high IV lets sold strikes sit farther away; variance means keep individual position risk small.

rules.text: A strike with about 16% chance of finishing ITM marks the one-standard-deviation boundary for that expiration; about 2.5% ITM marks two standard deviations.
In high IV, the same probability strikes sit much farther from the stock, which suits premium selling entries.
Because short-term results are noisy, keep individual position risk small and rely on many occurrences for outcomes to approach expectations.

stats.label: Outcomes within 1 SD
stats.conditions: Based on current implied volatility distribution

stats.label: Outcomes within 2 SD
stats.conditions: Based on current implied volatility distribution

stats.label: Outcomes within 3 SD
stats.conditions: Based on current implied volatility distribution

stats.label: Probability outside 1 SD (both sides)
stats.conditions: Half of this, about 16%, applies to one side

mechanics.point: Implied volatility is the annualized one-SD move; example: $100 stock at 20% IV gives $80-$120 (1SD), $60-$140 (2SD), $40-$160 (3SD) over a year. The expected-move formula scales this to the option's DTE.

Sell straddles at roughly 45 days to expiration, which tastylive research found balances shorter and longer durations.
Focus on probabilities at entry and keep the risk/reward relationship reasonable, since the short straddle includes a naked call with undefined risk.
