Selling a call and a put at the same strike and expiration to profit from stable prices and time decay.

concepts-strangle.summary: Covers long and short strangles (OTM call and put, same expiration), breakeven math, comparison with straddles, and the tastylive approach: sell about 45 DTE, take profit at 50% of credit, roll the untested side closer when the other side is breached.
unmapped: hedging a strangle by selling further OTM options

strategy_notes.max_profit: total premium collected, less trading costs
strategy_notes.max_loss: undefined; naked call side is unlimited, put side limited to stock reaching zero
strategy_notes.breakevens: upper = short call strike + net premium; lower = short put strike - net premium

tasty_setup.strikes: OTM both sides; higher IV lets strikes be wider for similar credit, or closer strikes for a much larger credit
tasty_setup.iv: sell when IV is high and stock expected to sit still

management.roll: when the tested side is breached, roll the untested side closer to the stock price; goal is collecting more premium to improve breakeven and reduce cost basis
management.defend: roll untested side closer when tested side is breached (studies showed this to be optimal)
management.close: buy back at 50% of credit

concepts-strike-price.summary: Defines strike price, moneyness (ITM/ATM/OTM), intrinsic versus extrinsic value, strike versus spot, and how outlook and risk appetite guide strike choice.

rules.text: Choose strikes by outlook and risk tolerance: expecting a big move favors a high-delta long call; expecting a small rise may favor a high-delta short put.
Risk-averse traders may prefer a long call over a short put since the long call loss is limited to premium; a bearish trader may likewise prefer a long put over a short call.
Watch ATM options closely near expiration since they resolve to ITM or OTM unless the stock closes exactly at the strike (pin).

mechanics.point: At expiration an option is ITM or OTM unless the underlying closes exactly at the strike (an ATM pin); ITM options are more likely exercised, OTM usually expire worthless.
Extrinsic (time) value rises with demand, for example when VIX rises, and falls when demand drops.
ATM options cost more than OTM because they have higher odds of finishing ITM.

terms.definition: The fixed price at which the option holder may buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying.
How far an option is in the money.
Option price beyond intrinsic value, mainly time and volatility.
Current market price of the underlying.

concepts-theta.summary: Theta is the daily decay of extrinsic value; hurts option buyers, helps sellers, grows toward expiration and is largest for ATM options. Positive theta does not guarantee profit.

rules.text: Judge theta relative to option price (e.g. as a percent of premium), not as an absolute number.
Do not assume positive theta guarantees profit; large adverse moves can cause big losses for sellers.

mechanics.point: Theta is quoted per day, typically negative for long options and positive for short. All else equal, decay accelerates as expiration nears.
ATM options carry the highest theta because they hold the most extrinsic value; deep ITM and deep OTM options have lower theta.
Theta can rise if extrinsic value is retained while time passes, e.g. an OTM option moves ATM or IV rises.
Example given: premium 2.00 and theta -0.05 means about 2.5% decay per day, viewed as relatively high.

terms.definition: Expected daily change in option price from time passing.
Position gains value as time passes, typical of short options.
Time and volatility value that decays to zero by expiration.

concepts-vega.summary: Vega measures option price sensitivity to a 1-point change in implied volatility; long options have positive vega, short options negative; vega is larger for longer-dated and ATM options.

rules.text: Expecting IV to rise favors owning higher-vega options; expecting IV to fall favors selling options or holding lower vega.
A fall in IV helps premium sellers, who can buy back for less, and hurts long premium positions.

mechanics.point: Vega is dollar change per share for a 1-point IV move; e.g. vega 0.05 on a $2.00 option at 20% IV implies $2.05 at 21% IV.
Vega is greater for longer maturities and for ATM versus OTM options.
IV is the market price of volatility; vega is the sensitivity to it.

terms.definition: Change in option price per 1% change in implied volatility.
Position gains when IV rises, as with owned options.

rules.text: Sell vertical spreads in high IV expecting contraction; buy verticals when IV rank is low to stay engaged and hedge short-vol exposure.

Credit spreads: avoid letting the spread go fully ITM; if the short option holds more extrinsic value than the long, roll out in time for a credit to cut max loss and raise max profit.

Legging out of a vertical changes defined risk to undefined risk (if short remains) and is usually not advised.

mechanics.point: VIX is built from S&P 500 options with between 23 and 37 days to expiry, ATM and OTM puts and calls, weighted into a 30-day expected volatility.
VIX is inversely correlated with the S&P 500: it rises in selloffs and trends lower in rallies or sideways markets.
The index itself is not tradable; exposure comes through VIX futures, VIX options, or ETPs such as VXX tracking short-term VIX futures.
VIX shows expected volatility; actual volatility can differ greatly, so traders also watch historical volatility.

concepts-volatility-skew.summary: Volatility skew is the uneven implied volatility across strikes and expirations. Normal equity skew is negative (OTM puts richer) from hedging demand; gold shows reverse skew. Skew is one input, not a standalone signal.

rules.text: Elevated IV does not automatically justify selling and depressed IV does not automatically justify buying; IV may be high for good reason.
Approach sharp changes in skew shape cautiously until you understand why it shifted.
Enter both legs of a spread as a single order at a net debit so one leg cannot fill without the other.
In positive (reverse) skew, covered calls can exploit inflated call premium.

mechanics.point: Negative skew: OTM puts have higher IV than ATM/ITM, the usual structure because of demand for downside protection. Positive/reverse skew: OTM calls richer, seen in gold as a safe haven. Neutral skew: flat IV across strikes.
Skew steepens when demand for downside protection rises and flattens when sentiment turns bullish; it reflects supply and demand and perceived risk.
Forward (term-structure/time) skew compares IV across expirations; near-term IV can spike before an event, flattening or inverting the structure.
Example bear put spread: buy the 100 put, sell the 90 put; max loss is the net debit, max gain is strike width minus debit below the lower strike.

concepts-vxx.summary: Describes VXX, an ETN holding front two VIX futures, and contrasts it with the VIX index: option style, settlement, time decay from contango, liquidity and tax treatment; notes VXX suits only short horizons.

rules.text: VXX is not a long-term holding; its futures rolls create persistent decay, so it only fits a very short horizon, and most traders prefer selling it.
tastylive studies indicate other volatility products are more efficient than VXX in most situations.
VXX options are American style and carry high early assignment risk, unlike European VIX options.
Volatility products are often best traded near the open and close and around major economic releases, when volatility tends to be higher.

mechanics.point: VXX holds the front two VIX futures with changing weights to approximate a constant 30-day VIX future; rolling causes decay in contango, and it can outperform VIX in backwardation.
VIX is a non-tradeable index with European, cash-settled options; VXX is an ETN with American, physically-delivered options (100 shares per contract); both are 1x leverage.
Options on both VIX (index) and VXX (non-equity) qualify for Section 1256 treatment: 60% long-term, 40% short-term.
VIX options liquidity is very high; VXX is slightly lower but still highly liquid.
An ETN cannot go negative; the most a VXX buyer can lose is the purchase price.
Barclays suspended VXX issuance on April 28, 2022, and filed a shelf registration on May 23, 2022 that allowed new issuance; VXX can still be bought.

terms.definition: An exchange-traded note tracking a blend of the front two VIX futures.
Upward-sloping futures curve that makes rolled VIX futures products lose value over time.

concepts-zebra.summary: ZEBRA (zero extrinsic value back ratio): buy two ITM options and sell one ATM option so extrinsic cost is offset, giving near 100 delta stock replacement with debit-limited loss; skew and expiration choice affect setup.

strategy_notes.legs: Call ZEBRA: buy 2 ITM calls, sell 1 ATM call. Put ZEBRA: buy 2 ITM puts, sell 1 ATM put. Sold option's extrinsic should cancel the total extrinsic in the two longs.
strategy_notes.outlook: Call ZEBRA bullish; put ZEBRA bearish

strategy_notes.max_loss: The debit paid (acts like an embedded stop loss, similar to a married put or married call).
strategy_notes.breakevens: Call: short call strike plus any extrinsic paid. Put: short put strike minus any extrinsic paid.

tasty_setup.iv: Low IV ideal.
tasty_setup.credit_target: Extrinsic collected from the short should equal total extrinsic of the two longs.

management.loss_rule: Max loss is the debit paid.

greeks.theta: No extrinsic to lose if set up properly.

Pursue long-term tax treatment or trade low-priced product with little extrinsic a few points ITM (longer-dated ZEBRA)
when_to_avoid: Paying extrinsic to get a cheaper trade: it decays and dampens profit as the trade moves ITM
mistakes: Leaving extrinsic value in the setup to save debit

rules.text: Make the extrinsic received from the ATM short equal the total extrinsic paid in the two ITM longs, i.e. long strike extrinsic is half of the short's premium.
Short-dated ZEBRA for brief directional moves with lower total risk; longer-dated when seeking long-term tax treatment or in low-priced products.
Prefer low IV environments for ZEBRAs.
